reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it reports an alleged backdoor in an arbitrage bot that drained users' Ethereum funds, rather than promoting participation in the bot. The narration describes an investigation, victims, and ongoing risk, and directs viewers to a news article for more information rather than requesting money, wallet access, or personal data. The transaction screenshots function as reporting context, not a demonstrated solicitation.

opening.argument: The video connects a crypto trading bot with an income promise and a concrete next step: following an external URL. It presents the bot as providing “stress-free passive income,” while directing viewers to “Follow the URL for the full article.” That pairing can function as a participation funnel even when the wording is framed as reporting: the audience is shown a bot-based profit opportunity and then sent onward to information about it. The description also repeats the arbitrage-trading and funds language alongside an external link, reinforcing that the link is attached to the financial subject rather than being incidental.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the destination a news article does not eliminate the action being solicited: viewers are still directed to follow an external URL after being shown a bot associated with passive income. The narration’s investigative wording also repeats the bot’s income proposition, so the financial opportunity remains salient even if the video does not explicitly say “deposit.” The evidence therefore supports a promotional pathway without requiring an explicit wallet request.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited material shows only that the video reports a claim and directs viewers to an article. It does not tell viewers to activate, fund, configure, or trade with the bot, and “Follow the URL for the full article” identifies an informational destination rather than a participation instruction. The income language is explicitly presented as part of the alleged conduct being investigated, not as an offer made by the video.

citations.quote: An investigation of AmivBots' contract revealed a backdoor that allows the creators to drain Ether from its users wallets.
Follow the URL for the full article

opening.argument: Several high-risk signals appear together: a bot-based trading mechanism, passive-income language, a striking $28,029 user result, Ethereum-related contracts, and visible address-to-address transfers. The frames show “Our user made $28,029” alongside Ethereum contract language, while other frames show repeated transfers in a From/To transaction interface. Separately, the narration describes an arbitrage bot that claims passive income. Taken together, these are not neutral finance references: they combine automated crypto trading, an unusually attractive result, and transaction activity in a way that can make the bot appear profitable and operational.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The warning framing does not neutralize the promotional force of the signals shown. A viewer encounters a specific five-figure user result, Ethereum contracts, and repeated transfers while also hearing that the bot automates trading for profits. Even if the video calls the mechanism dangerous, displaying a compelling outcome and operational-looking transaction activity can still normalize the underlying bot as a real route to returns.

citations.quote: Arbitrage bots are programs that automate trading for profits based on historical market information.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The visual snippets do not establish that the displayed amount came from this bot, that it was received by a viewer, or that the transfers represent profit. The narration explicitly says the bot was draining users’ funds through a backdoor, so the transaction display is consistent with investigative evidence rather than a returns demonstration. No frame or text gives a funding or activation instruction.

opening.argument: Although the video adopts the language of an investigation, its structure can still operate as promotion for the underlying bot. It explains that arbitrage bots automate trading for profits, highlights a claimed “stress-free passive income” model, displays a user result of $28,029, and directs viewers to an external article. The warning language supplies credibility and attention while the profit-oriented details make the bot concrete and attractive. Presenting the product, its claimed benefit, and a route to more information can steer viewers toward participation even when the speaker describes a backdoor as harmful.

Calling the bot dangerous may increase its perceived reality and visibility without preventing viewers from seeking it out.
